topic: Blue whale heart: 2 bpm on dives, surface racing, 180 kg heart, size limit
hook: Blue whale hearts can beat twice a minute

slides.title: 2 beats per minute
slides.body: Scientists suction-cupped a sensor to a wild blue whale. On deep dives, its heart dropped to just 2 beats a minute.
slides.image_prompt: A huge blue whale diving into dark deep ocean water, faint sunbeams fading above, calm and silent atmosphere

slides.title: Then it races
slides.body: Back at the surface, it jumped to 25–37 beats a minute to reload oxygen fast, close to its maximum.
slides.image_prompt: A blue whale breaking the ocean surface, spray of breath rising into bright air, waves around its back

slides.title: A 180 kg heart
slides.body: A blue whale heart preserved in Canada weighs about 180 kg, roughly as much as two adult men.
slides.image_prompt: A giant preserved red whale heart displayed in a museum case, dramatic lighting, scale shown by a small chair beside it

slides.title: Too big to grow?
slides.body: Researchers think its heart already works near its limits, which may help explain why no animal has grown bigger.
slides.image_prompt: Aerial view of an enormous blue whale in deep blue ocean, tiny boat far away for scale

caption:
In 2018, Stanford researchers stuck a sensor on a wild blue whale in Monterey Bay. While it dove for food, its heart slowed to just 2 beats a minute. Back at the surface, it raced to 37.

The study suggests the biggest animal ever may already be pushing its heart to the limit. That could be one reason nothing alive has grown larger. Source: Goldbogen et al., PNAS 2019.
